add.issue.comment.md:
Review of PR #383 (claude/hugo). The design is right and the `stale`/`dead`/`clean` split is the correct narrowing. One blocking defect, one coverage gap, one claim that does not hold.

**Blocking: an unparseable lock is read as `dead`, and now unwinds a live holder's rebase.**

`claimOver(null)` returns `'dead'`, and `write()` uses `fs.writeFileSync(path, data, {flag:'wx'})` — an exclusive *create* followed by a separate write. Between those two syscalls the lock file exists and is empty. A second process that loses the `wx` race reads it right then, parses nothing, calls the holder dead, breaks the lock, and — new in this branch — aborts the rebase the live holder is running.

A/B, same probe, rebase in progress plus a zero-length `epiq-sync.lock`:

- merge-base `9f58cca4`: sync refuses, `rebase in progress` still there.
- `75e20541`: sync succeeds, rebase state gone.

That is the one outcome the change set out to prevent, and the existing first test misses it because it writes a well-formed lock. P5VM0FE point 7 already records that `isProcessAlive` is unreliable in the container; this is the same doubt from the other side, and here it is destructive rather than merely slow.

Minimal fix: `if (!holder) return 'stale';` in `claimOver`. A truncated lock still gets broken, so nothing wedges — it just stops being grounds for unwinding somebody's rebase. Making the write atomic (temp file + `linkSync`) closes the window itself and is the fuller fix.

**`clearStaleGitLocks` has no test.** It is only named in `sync.ts`; no test writes an `index.lock`. That was the review finding that moved the clearing to the top of `ensureSyncReady`, so it is the part most worth pinning. I confirmed by hand that it works — an `index.lock` in the worktree gitdir no longer wedges a sync — but per the project rule every fix gets a test that is red without it.

**The "three fail on main" claim is off.** Four fail on the merge base, and only two fail on the bug:

- `lock names a process that is gone` — throws the guard's message. Genuine.
- `crashed process left no lock behind` — same. Genuine.
- `broken on age from a live holder` — `AssertionError`, expected message to contain `rebase in progress`. Main already behaves correctly here.
- the merge test — same, `merge in progress`.

So two of the five are coupled to the reworded message rather than to behaviour. They would not catch a regression in the clearing logic. Worth asserting the operation is still present (they do) and dropping the message coupling, or keeping it knowingly.

**Also:** `clearStaleGitLocks` only reads the worktree gitdir, so a `refs/heads/…lock` in the common gitdir survives. Filed separately as a gap, not a blocker — I could not make it wedge a sync in a probe.

**Still open:** this ticket is tagged `human-input-needed` and the fork it names — recover vs refuse-but-explain vs a deliberate repair command — has not been answered. The branch takes the first option. That is the user's call to confirm before merge, not mine.

Branch is 3 commits behind `origin/main` (`221e158c`); none of them touch these files, so the rebase is clean.

add.issue.name: clearStaleGitLocks misses ref locks in the common gitdir

edit.description.md:
From the review of PR #383 / branch `TATEM5B-sync-recovery`.

`clearStaleGitLocks` resolves its directory with `getGitDir`, which for a linked worktree returns the *worktree's* gitdir (`.git/worktrees/<name>`). It then sweeps `*.lock` at that top level only. That covers `index.lock`, `HEAD.lock` and `MERGE_MSG.lock`, which is the common case and the one TATEM5B was about.

It does not cover the common gitdir. A git killed while updating a branch ref leaves `refs/heads/<state branch>.lock` there, and `packed-refs.lock` and `config.lock` live there too. Those survive the clearing, and a later `git rebase` that needs the same ref fails with "cannot lock ref" — the same shape of permanent wedge TATEM5B fixed, reached by a narrower path.

Not demonstrated harmful. A probe on the branch that planted `refs/heads/epiq/state.lock` in the common gitdir still synced successfully, because that sync had no ref update to make. So this is a reasoned gap, not a reproduced failure, and it wants a repro before a fix.

If it is worth closing, the same `clean`/`dead` claim gates it — the caller already knows nobody is in the worktree. The care needed is that the common gitdir is shared with the user's own repository and every other worktree, so a sweep there must be scoped to the state branch's own ref, never a blanket `*.lock` walk.

add.issue.comment.md:
Re-read at `7c0e8278` (claude/hugo). Both fixes to the first blocker are right — `claimOver(null)` is `stale`, and `linkSync` from a per-process temp name closes the window rather than tolerating it. The suite is green here too: 9 passing, 11s.

**New blocker, introduced by the sweep: `clearStaleGitLocks` deletes the sync lock the calling process is holding.**

`LOCK_FILE` is `epiq-sync.lock`, and it lives in the worktree gitdir — the same directory the sweep walks, removing everything that ends in `.lock`. So it matches.

Probe on `7c0e8278`: acquire the lock the way sync does, then make exactly the call `ensureSyncReady` makes.

```
{ "claim": "clean",
  "lockExistsBeforeSweep": true,
  "lockExistsAfterSweep": false,
  "removed": ["epiq-sync.lock"] }
```

This is not an edge case — it is the ordinary path. The clearing runs whenever `claim !== 'stale'`, which is every normal sync, and it happens near the top of `ensureSyncReady`. Everything after it — bootstrap, fetch, rebase, commit, push — runs with no lock on disk. A second process arriving during that window reads no lock, claims `clean`, and is then licensed to clear git locks and abort the rebase the first one is running. That is TATEM5B's own failure, promoted from a microsecond race to the default path.

The three new lock tests miss it because none of them holds the sync lock while sweeping. `leaves a worktree with none of them alone` asserts `[]`, which is true only because no lock is held at that moment; under a real sync that list is always `['epiq-sync.lock']`. `do not stop a sync that finds them` runs a real sync but asserts only that it succeeded and `index.lock` is gone, never that the sync lock survived.

Fix: exclude the sync lock from the sweep — `clearStaleGitLocks(cwd, {preserve: [LOCK_FILE]})`, or skip the name outright. Not by renaming the lock: the name is how two epiq processes find each other's claims, so an old build and a new one would stop seeing each other.

For the regression test, the sweep has to be exercised *with the lock held* — the probe above is the shape. A sync-level version would assert the lock file still exists at the point the rebase runs.

**Nit, read from the code and not tested:** a process SIGKILLed between `writeFileSync(pending)` and `linkSync` leaves `epiq-sync.lock.<pid>` in the gitdir forever. It does not end in `.lock`, so the sweep never takes it, and nothing else does either. Harmless litter, but it accumulates in the one directory this code is careful about.

**On the fork:** thanks for recording the answer — that resolves what I flagged. I had no way to see the decision from here, only the tag.

**On the count:** your reframing is the right one. "Fails on main" was never the measure for the two guards, since main refuses everything; red against a loosened branch is what actually pins them.

add.issue.name: A `clean` lock claim licenses unwinding a rebase, but only proves nobody claimed the worktree

edit.description.md:
From the review of PR #383 / TATEM5B, raised after the two blockers were fixed. Not a defect in that branch — a question about the rule it establishes.

TATEM5B lets a sync clear an abandoned rebase when its `LockClaim` is `clean` or `dead`. Those two are not equally strong evidence:

- `dead` is a positive statement from the operating system that a named process is gone.
- `clean` says only that **no lock file was on disk**. That is the absence of a claim, not the absence of an occupant.

Anything that enters the state worktree without taking the sync lock is indistinguishable from an empty worktree, and is therefore eligible to have its rebase aborted under it.

**The concrete case is already shipped.** `loadProject`'s boot pull rebased the state worktree with no lock at all; PR #383 fixes that, but every epiq binary released before it still does the unlocked pull. So: a stale `~/.local/bin/epiq` (or an older GUI/MCP/TUI) doing its first-boot rebase on a fresh clone, while a current build syncs, gives no lock on disk → `clean` → the current build aborts the older one's live rebase. Fixing `loadProject` cannot close this, because the old builds are already out there.

The window is narrow — it needs a clone with no `init.workspace` event yet, a first boot, and a concurrent sync — and it was not reproduced. It is recorded because it is the one direction the `stale` reasoning was careful about, reached by a path that reasoning does not cover.

**The options, for a decision rather than a guess:**

1. **Leave it.** `clean` keeps licensing recovery. Simplest, and the narrowness may be the right answer, especially once everyone has upgraded past the `loadProject` fix.
2. **License unwinding on `dead` only.** `clean` still takes the worktree and still clears git's own `*.lock` files, but does not abort a rebase — the same shape of restraint already chosen for `stale`. Costs: a crash that left no lock behind stops self-healing, which is one of the cases `sync-recovery.test.ts` currently pins as recovered.
3. **Make `clean` mean more.** Require a second signal before unwinding under `clean` — rebase state older than some age, or no recent mtime in the worktree.

Option 2 is the conservative one and the cheapest to reason about; option 1 is defensible. The trade in 2 is real and is why this is not being decided in the review: it gives up recovery in exactly the "crashed process left no lock behind" case.

Related: [[QR97TP3]]. The advisory nature of the lock is unchanged by any of these — a person running git by hand in the state worktree is outside all of it.

add.issue.comment.md:
Verified at `f17ae9ac` (claude/hugo): blocker closed. Dropped `preserve: [SYNC_LOCK_FILE]` in a throwaway worktree and reran — 1 failed, 11 passed, and the failure is exactly `the sync lock went missing while the sync was still running`. Only the watcher goes red, so the read that the two helper-level tests were not carrying the weight is right. Restored: 12/12 in 10.7s. CI green on this head, all five jobs.

Also checked the flake risk a 2ms poller invites — a tick landing after the lock releases but before `clearInterval`, which would be a false red in the gate. It cannot happen: `withSyncLock` releases in its `finally` and there is no await between that and `syncEpiqWithRemote` returning, so the continuation and the `clearInterval` run in one synchronous block.

Nothing outstanding from the review on this branch.

One thing raised separately rather than here, because it is about the rule and not the code: `C8J7VKY`. `dead` and `clean` are not equally strong evidence — `clean` proves only that nobody wrote a lock, not that nobody is in the worktree — and the unlocked boot pull this PR fixes still exists in every already-released binary, which no change here can reach. Narrow and unreproduced, tagged `human-input-needed` with three options. It does not block this merge.

add.issue.comment.md:
claude/hugo. The recycling path holds — I traced it rather than taking it: acquiring on `stale` does `rmSync(lockPath)` then writes the breaker's own holder, and `release()` removes that because the pid matches. So the file really is gone afterwards and the next sync really does see `clean`. Under option 2 nothing clears it from then on. That is a genuine hole in option 2 as written, and it moves my lean: option 2 is only safe **paired** with something, not on its own.

On the pairing you suggest — recording the holder's start time beside its pid — two costs, measured here on darwin:

- `ps -o lstart= -p <pid>` has **one-second granularity** (`Sun Sep 20 11:29:02 2026`). A pid recycled inside the same second still matches, so it narrows the window rather than closing it. Linux `/proc/<pid>/stat` field 22 is far finer, so the two platforms would not be equally strong.
- It puts a **subprocess spawn** on the lock-acquisition path, which today is filesystem calls plus `process.kill(pid, 0)`. Autosync takes this path every few seconds.

**A fourth option worth weighing, because it drops pid identity entirely:** have the holder refresh the lock while it works — rewrite or `utimes` it every second or two — and make liveness "refreshed recently" rather than "a process with that number answers". A recycled pid then cannot look alive, because the recycled process is not refreshing this file.

What that buys beyond the pairing:

- No subprocess, no `/proc`, no per-platform difference.
- It fixes the **cross-machine** case, which today can never yield `dead` at all: `claimOver` short-circuits on `hostname !== os.hostname()` and falls back to the ten-minute age backstop. A refreshed lock is readable by any machine that can see the file.
- `dead` becomes a positive statement again, which is what option 2 needs to carry the rule alone.

What it costs: a timer for the length of a sync, and a judgement about how long "recently" is — too tight and a process paused on an unreachable remote gets declared dead, which is the failure this whole area is about. That argues for a generous multiple of the refresh interval, and it is the part that would need thinking through rather than picking a number.

I have not implemented or measured any of this beyond the `ps` granularity above — it is a design suggestion, on the same reasoned-not-observed footing as the two paths already on this ticket.

For whoever decides: the shape of the choice is now *is `clean` weak evidence* (options 1–3) and, if it is, *what makes `dead` strong enough to stand alone* (the start-time pairing, or the refresh above). Those are two decisions, and the second only matters if the first goes against `clean`.

add.issue.comment.md:
claude/hugo. Checked the event-loop claim and it is right: `runGit` uses `spawn` with a promise resolved from its callbacks, not `spawnSync`, so the loop is free for the whole of any git call and a refresh timer keeps firing through a hanging fetch. Option 4's cost is softer than I wrote it.

One more fact that narrows it further, and it is measured from the constants rather than reasoned: **git calls here are already bounded.** `GIT_TIMEOUT_MS` is 10s, `GIT_SLOW_TIMEOUT_MS` is 120s for the network ones. So "paused on an unreachable remote" is not indefinite — it is at most a couple of minutes per call, and the sync fails rather than hanging.

Taken together, the interval question is smaller than I made it sound. What a refresh has to survive is a scheduling hiccup, not a stalled network, and the ceiling is the ten minutes the current backstop already costs. That is a wide bracket, and picking inside it is closer to a default than a judgement.

What would still be worth confirming before building on it: epiq does some synchronous filesystem work on this path (`snapshotEventLogs`, the merged-event reads), and a large enough event log could starve a one-second timer for longer than expected. Milliseconds on any log seen so far, but it is the one thing that could make a refresh miss while the process is perfectly healthy — so it wants a measurement on a large board rather than an assumption.

That is the whole of my input on this ticket. The decision is unchanged in shape: whether `clean` is weak evidence, and if so what makes `dead` strong enough alone.
